क्या आपने कभी किसी से सुना है —

"आँख तिरछी है? कोई बात नहीं, बड़े होते-होते सीधी हो जाएगी।"

मैं समझता हूँ कि यह बात कहाँ से आती है। बड़े-बुज़ुर्गों का अनुभव, पड़ोसी की सलाह, या कभी-कभी किसी डॉक्टर की भी राय।

लेकिन सच यह है —

भेंगापन अपने आप ठीक नहीं होता।

जब एक आँख टेढ़ी होती है, तो दिमाग उस आँख की छवि को नज़रअंदाज़ करने लगता है। धीरे-धीरे उस आँख की रोशनी कम होती जाती है — और एक उम्र के बाद इसे वापस लाना बहुत मुश्किल हो जाता है।

वह उम्र है — 7 से 8 साल।

इससे पहले इलाज हो जाए, तो नतीजे बेहद अच्छे होते हैं।
चश्मा, patching, या surgery — जो भी ज़रूरी हो।

अगर आपके बच्चे की आँख में कुछ अलग दिखे — तो एक बार किसी specialist से ज़रूर मिलें।

Mumbai में clinic और पूरे भारत में teleconsult उपलब्ध है।
📍 Link to book — comments में।

To every parent in a NICU right now — this post is for you.

ROP is a condition that affects the developing blood vessels in the retina of premature babies. It has no visible symptoms. Babies don't show any signs of discomfort. The only way to know if your baby has it is a screening examination by a trained specialist.

Most babies who are screened have mild or no ROP. Most mild cases resolve on their own.

But when ROP is severe and goes undetected — it can cause permanent vision loss. Even blindness.

And here's the reality in India: many families are discharged from the NICU without a clear ROP referral. Not because anyone was careless. But because NICUs are stretched, parents are overwhelmed, and ROP screening can fall through the cracks.

If your baby was born before 34 weeks, or weighed less than 2000 grams at birth:

👉 Ask your neonatologist today: "Has my baby been referred for an ROP eye check?"
👉 If yes — do not miss the follow-up appointments, even if your baby seems fine.
👉 If no — ask for a referral immediately.

I'm Dr Ashish Doshi, a pediatric ophthalmologist and ROP specialist in Mumbai. I work in close coordination with NICU teams and see babies for screening and treatment.

Consultations are available in-clinic in Mumbai and via teleconsult for families anywhere in India.

If you have questions — DM me, or visit squinteyedoctor.in

featured_reviews.name: Renu Chudamani
featured_reviews.review_text:
My mother recently had her cataract operation done at Ayush / Dr Agarwal’s eye clinic. Here’s an honest review of her experience.

1. Location: 5-stars - the location of the clinic is conveniently right at the beginning of postal colony, and although some road work was going on further down, it didn’t impact our ability to get in and out of the clinic with ease. The clinic is located on the first floor, even though there are 3 elevators, taking the stairs might be easier than the long wait for the elevator.
2. Facility: 4-stars: The entire place is kept very clean and tidy by a group of busy house keeping staff. The only gripe I had was the bathrooms did have an issue with water running from one of the hoses in the one stall. I also saw did see a cockroach (!!). However, I must say that when house cleaning was informed they took action right away.
3. Convenience: 5-stars: All in one clinic, you have your consultations, eye prescriptions, all ophthalmologist  related tests as well as two operating rooms make this truly a convenient experience. No need to run to another location to get anything.
4. Wait times: 4-5- stars: Varies, although we were seen within 15-20min for most of our appointments. On the day of the surgery we were seen almost right away.
5. Doctors: 5-stars: Dr Nita Shah is amazing, loved her calm reassuring demeanor and she was a realist, she didn’t try to give any false promises. She answered questions patiently even after a busy day of operations and seeing patients in the OPD. Stellar attitude, totally recommend this doctor!
6. Front-house/Triage Staff: 5-stars:  Ms Amrita went out of her way to help my mother, and comfort her about the procedure. She was patient with any questions, and helped square away questions about insurance, and what needed to be sent over. She even was able to help us offline with questions over WhatsApp. Really appreciated her help, and she was a big reason for why my mother wanted to get her cataract done at this location. Always smiling, fast and efficient, she truly is a star employee. Ms Snehanka was also a great help, she worked quickly to get us out of the hospital post surgery helping get prescriptions filled and ensuring payments are done on time.
7. Nurses: 4-stars: I think it’s here that the hospital can do some more work. The nurses are a little disorganized and although I think they’re all pretty competent it would be good for a ticketing system or something similar rather than someone calling out your name when your expected to move from station to station. On multiple occasions I saw that they mispronounced the patient names (no fault of theirs!!) but this led to some confusion. Also, there was some attitude from some of the nurses, I realize they had a heavy workload, so maybe something to look into with training and the hours they’re working.

Overall my mom had  great experience, pre and post op. Thank you!
P.S: One thing I did want to mention - they do have a screen up so you can watch your loved one’s cataract operation while it’s happening. Not for the faint of heart, and completely optional, it’s only through the window to the exclusive waiting room for patients that you can view this.

Thank you for your response. I would like to clarify a few things further:

1. Regarding the insistence on surgery:
While I appreciate your clarification, the fact remains that my initial query was regarding lenses, not surgery. The suggestion of LASIK surgery was made without taking my actual concern into consideration, which felt like an insistence on a different treatment.

I understand that you were sharing a fact about CGHS coverage. However, the way it was conveyed—specifically the eye-roll and the tone—felt rude and dismissive. A simple fact can be stated in a respectful and professional manner, without conveying irritation. My concern is not about the fact itself but the delivery.

3. Dismissing us after mentioning affordability:
When my father expressed that we could not afford the surgery, the immediate dismissal of us from the consultation felt unprofessional. Instead of discussing alternative options or even providing some guidance, we were effectively shown the door. This is what I meant by being dismissed.

4. False promises or commitments:
While I agree that false promises should not be made, professionalism involves handling all patients with respect and care, especially when they raise concerns. In our case, the conversation could have been handled with more patience and understanding, and alternatives could have been suggested instead of just ending the interaction.

5. Professionalism and respect:
I believe professionalism goes beyond just giving facts; it also includes how we make patients feel during consultations. In this instance, the interaction left us feeling dismissed rather than respected or valued as patients. A more considerate and understanding approach would have made a positive difference.

Edit 2 -

It’s quite surprising to see how delusional one can be. At no point did I claim that Dr Ashar discussed charges or financial solutions with us. My concern was about his dismissive attitude and the way he handled our query.

Firmness and being straight to the point are not the issues here. The problem is the lack of courtesy and professionalism displayed during the interaction. Rolling one’s eyes, speaking irritably, and dismissing patients when they express financial constraints are not examples of firmness—they are examples of rude behaviour.

If you are unwilling to acknowledge this, that’s your prerogative, but dismissing genuine concerns as a misunderstanding or misrepresentation reflects poorly on the ability to take accountability.
